zh.title: 小引 · 一部书，和七组反对
zh.deck: 六个沉思之外，还有作者主动请来、亲手编入书中的反对声音。

sections.heading: 一部书
paragraphs: 笛卡尔是十七世纪的法国人，后来的二十来年住在荷兰，《第一哲学沉思集》是在那里写成的，一六四一年出版。
正文很薄，六篇，叫六个沉思。
它用第一人称写。开篇那个我坐在火炉边，穿着冬天的袍子，手里捏着一张纸。他说，凡是能怀疑的，我都要怀疑一遍，看看剩下什么。
六篇是接连的日子。第四篇开头他写，我这几天已经把心灵从感官那边领开惯了；后面又回头说前几天那些夸大的怀疑。一本讲怀疑的书，写成了一个人连着几天坐在那里的样子。
他要找的东西，他自己有个说法：阿基米德只要一个牢牢不动的点，就能把整个地球撬离原处；我若能找到哪怕最小的一样靠得住又摇不动的，也就可以指望大事了。

sections.heading: 顺带说一句那句名言
paragraphs: 有人是带着我思故我在来读这本书的。
六个沉思里没有这句话。那里的说法是：我是，我存在。后面紧跟着一句：每当我说出它，或者在心里想到它，它必然是真的。
这句话自己带着条件。每一回说出它，或者想到它，它就撤不掉。
可这句名言在这本书里也不是没有。它在这本书里头一次出现，是在第一组反驳里，出自反驳者卡特鲁斯之手，而且是当作笛卡尔的话引的：他说，我思，所以我在。笛卡尔自己用它，是在答第二组的时候，为的是说明一件事：这不是一个三段论，不靠先有凡在思想的都存在那一条，是心灵一眼看见的。

sections.heading: 七组反对
paragraphs: 真正少见的在后头。
稿子写完，他没有直接拿去印。付印之前，稿子先送到几位有才学的人手里，请他们审。头一组是一位神父写的，经两位朋友转到他手上；别的几组，照他自己的说法，是梅森神父向很多人发了挑战，从一些人那里要到的。
第一版印进了六组反驳，连同他逐条的答辩；第二版又添了一组。
第二版的书名页上写着：另附若干博学之士的各种反驳，连同作者的答辩。说是另附，篇幅却远远超过六个沉思。一本书的大半，是别人在打它，和作者在挡。
七组里有当时的大人物，霍布斯是一组，阿尔诺是一组，伽桑狄是一组。组也不都是一个人，有的一组通篇自称我们。
七组也不是各自对着同一本书开火。至少第五组读过前面的反驳，第六组读过前面的答辩。

sections.heading: 两副面孔
paragraphs: 还有一件得先说明。
这部书有两副面孔。上面说的是拉丁文的两版；法文本一六四七年出。
法文本不是拉丁本的影子。两边有差，而那些差别在这本书里本身就是题目：有一组反驳在法文本里被挪了位子，有一个词在两种文字里，都跟对方的原话对不上。下面有两篇专讲这个。
本系列引文保留底稿的译述，并以亚当与塔纳里编《笛卡尔全集》第七卷的拉丁文本、第九卷的法文与编者说明，以及卡昂大学的笛卡尔数字文库复核。之五另用到一份一六五〇年的转述，那一篇里会说明。

sections.heading: 下面六篇
paragraphs: 六篇讲的都是这一套安排上看得见的事：他为什么要印反对，这套安排怎么转，以及它转起来之后，有哪些落到了别人手里。
每篇末了另有一则旁注，拿一个当代的框架跟他并排放一下，那个框架叫 SAE。旁注是旁注，不是论证，可以跳过不读。

notes: 本文区分六篇《沉思》与一同出版的《反驳与答辩》。拉丁文初版为1641年，1642年第二版增入第七组；1647年法文本的编排另有差别。引文为本系列的译述，不借用现代中译本措辞。
正文与反驳的篇幅比例随版本和计量方式变化，这里保留后者远长于前者这一阅读事实，不把固定倍数当作各版共同的属性。

en.title: A Book, and Seven Sets of Objections
en.deck: Before publishing his Meditations, Descartes invited people to attack them. He put their attacks inside the book.

sections.heading: The book
paragraphs: René Descartes was a seventeenth-century French philosopher who spent much of his later working life in the Netherlands. He wrote the Meditations on First Philosophy there; it was first published in 1641.

The main text is short: six pieces, called six meditations. They are written in the first person. Near the beginning, the speaker sits by a fire in a winter gown, holding a sheet of paper. He is going to doubt whatever can be doubted and see whether anything remains.

The thinking has the shape of successive days. In the Fourth Meditation, he says he has lately grown accustomed to drawing his mind away from the senses. Later he looks back on the exaggerated doubts of the preceding days. A philosophical inquiry becomes the experience of someone sitting there, returning to the work.

He describes what he wants through Archimedes: give Archimedes one fixed and immovable point, and he could shift the earth. Let this thinker find even the smallest thing that is certain and unshakable, and he too may hope for something considerable.

sections.heading: Before the familiar quotation
paragraphs: Many readers arrive carrying the words “I think, therefore I am.” Those are not the words of the six meditations themselves. There the formulation is “I am, I exist,” followed by a qualification: whenever I utter it or conceive it in my mind, it must be true.
The qualification belongs to the claim. Each time it is thought or said, it cannot be withdrawn at that very moment.

But the familiar formula does appear elsewhere in the volume. Its first appearance comes in the First Objections, where Caterus quotes it as Descartes’ claim: I think, therefore I am. Descartes uses it himself in the Second Replies, to explain that it is not a syllogism. One does not first establish a general premise that everything which thinks exists, then apply it. The mind recognizes the connection directly.

sections.heading: The objections
paragraphs: The unusual part comes after the meditations. Descartes did not simply finish his manuscript and send it to a printer. Before publication, it went to learned readers for examination. A priest wrote the first objections, conveyed through two friends. Other sets followed a challenge circulated by Marin Mersenne, who solicited responses from a number of people.
The first edition included six sets of objections and Descartes’ replies. The second added a seventh. The title page announced objections by learned men, together with the author’s answers.
An appendix, apparently. Yet these exchanges occupy far more space than the six meditations. Most of the volume consists of people attacking the argument and its author answering them.

Some were formidable names: Hobbes, Arnauld, Gassendi. Nor does one set always mean one person; some speak throughout as “we.” And they were not all responding in isolation to the same untouched manuscript. At least the fifth set had seen earlier objections, and the sixth had seen earlier replies. The conversation was already affecting what later participants could say.

sections.heading: Two faces of the same book
paragraphs: One distinction matters from the outset. That account concerns the Latin editions. A French edition appeared in 1647, and it is not simply the Latin book reflected in another language.

The differences themselves become part of this series. One set of objections changes position. One word fails to match the opponent’s original wording in both languages. Two of the essays will stay with those details.

The readings retain the Chinese manuscript’s renderings, checked against the Latin text in volume VII of the Adam–Tannery edition, the French text and editorial explanations in volume IX, and the University of Caen’s digital Descartes corpus. Essay Five also relies on a report published in 1650; its indirect and adversarial character is made explicit there.

sections.heading: The six essays
paragraphs: These pieces follow what can be seen in the arrangement of the book: why Descartes wanted objections printed, how his arrangement worked, and what happened when parts of it passed into other people’s hands.

An optional note after each essay places a contemporary framework, SAE, beside the passage. These are comparisons, not proofs of one philosophy by another. They can be left unread. The book and the people arguing inside it come first.

notes: The six Meditations are distinguished from the Objections and Replies published with them. The 1641 Latin edition contained six sets of objections; the 1642 edition added a seventh. The French edition of 1647 has a different arrangement.
Passages are rendered afresh for these essays. The relative length of the main text and the exchanges depends on edition and counting method; no fixed ratio is asserted for every edition.
